analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to pay Medicare rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House committees for the rest of the 113th Congress, with 34 Democrats signed on and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Medicare drug benefit, low-income enrollees' drug costs are largely paid by taxpayers, but drug makers do not have to give the government the deep rebates they give Medicaid. This bill would force manufacturers to sign rebate agreements for drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees — roughly matching the Medicaid rebate — or have their drugs excluded from Medicare Part D coverage entirely. The rebates would go back into the Medicare prescription drug account.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who fund Medicare's low-income drug subsidies, and low-income Medicare enrollees (people eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid) whose drug coverage depends on those subsidies. A similar rebate rule already applies to drugs sold through Medicaid; this bill extends it to Medicare Part D drugs dispensed to the poorest enrollees.

how_it_helps.text: Requires drug manufacturers to pay the government a rebate for each covered Part D drug dispensed to a low-income ('rebate eligible') enrollee, calculated as the amount by which the Medicaid rebate exceeds the average rebate the manufacturer already gives Part D plans [S3].
Any manufacturer that refuses to sign a rebate agreement would have its drugs excluded from Medicare Part D coverage, giving it a strong reason to comply [S2].
Rebate payments must be deposited into the Medicare Prescription Drug Account, so the savings would offset Medicare drug spending rather than going elsewhere [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would pay rebates on a large volume of drugs now sold at higher prices to low-income enrollees whose costs are publicly subsidized. Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers would take on new reporting duties, with civil fines up to $10,000 a day for late or false reports.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a complex rebate calculation on top of the private, negotiated Part D system, with detailed per-drug, per-strength reporting by plans and estimated-then-reconciled rebate amounts — significant administrative burden for manufacturers and plans [S3].

Manufacturers could respond to lower net revenue by raising launch prices or reducing discounts, and the bill's own structure anticipates disputes by allowing the Secretary to base rebates on estimates with later reconciliation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is clear: money now flowing to manufacturers from publicly subsidized purchases of drugs for the poorest enrollees would flow back to Medicare instead. The design deliberately shields Medicaid pricing rules from the new rebates, and keeps the private Part D structure intact, but the formula and reporting machinery are complicated, and some of the cost could surface in higher prices elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to their health subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman and four other House Democrats introduced the Medicare Drug Savings Act of 2013 on April 16, 2013 [S1].
The House referred it to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
In April and June 2013 it was referred to the health subcommittees of those two committees, and the record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress [S5].
All 34 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they kept selling to publicly subsidized low-income Medicare enrollees without paying the Medicaid-style rebates this bill would have required. Taxpayers and low-income enrollees did not get the savings.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat, and the bill never moved in the Republican-controlled committees; no Republican is recorded in support [S4].

industries.note: They would have to pay Medicaid-style rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income Part D enrollees — sales that are heavily taxpayer-funded — or lose Part D coverage for their drugs. Their gain under the status quo is higher public spending on their drugs.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: They face new reporting requirements and fines for late or false reports, but the bill does not change their rebate arrangements or their role administering the benefit.
The rebate formula uses the Medicaid rebate amount, which is much smaller for non-innovator drugs, so most of the cost falls on brand-name manufacturers; generic makers' exposure is limited.
